title: 109. Quantitative Relationships & Measurement: Scale Factors in Maps and Drawings
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.learningObjective: Determine the actual distance represented by a map length using a given scale.
questions.question: A map has scale \(1:50{,}000\). What actual distance in metres does \(1\text{ cm}\) on the map represent?
questions.explanation: A scale of \(1:50{,}000\) means \(1\text{ cm}\) on the map represents \(50{,}000\text{ cm}\) in reality. Since \(100\text{ cm}=1\text{ m}\), \(50{,}000\text{ cm}=500\text{ m}\). The alternative \(50\text{ m}\) converts using \(1{,}000\) centimetres per metre instead of \(100\).
questions.hint: Express the real and drawing lengths in compatible units first.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate an actual length from a scale drawing.
questions.question: A drawing uses scale \(1:20\). A line on the drawing is \(6\text{ cm}\) long. What is the actual length in centimetres?
questions.explanation: A scale of \(1:20\) means \(1\text{ cm}\) on the drawing represents \(20\text{ cm}\) in reality. Therefore, \(6\text{ cm}\) on the drawing represents \(6\times 20=120\text{ cm}\). The alternative \(12\text{ cm}\) multiplies by \(2\) rather than the scale denominator \(20\).
questions.hint: Decide whether you are moving from the drawing to reality or the reverse.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate a map distance from an actual distance using a given scale.
questions.question: A map has scale \(1:200{,}000\). An actual distance is \(10\text{ km}\). What is the distance on the map in centimetres?
questions.explanation: Convert \(10\text{ km}\) to centimetres: \(10\times 100{,}000=1{,}000{,}000\text{ cm}\). Then divide by the scale factor: \(1{,}000{,}000\div 200{,}000=5\). Thus the map distance is \(5\text{ cm}\). The alternative \(50\text{ cm}\) uses a scale denominator of \(20{,}000\), dropping a zero from \(200{,}000\).
questions.hint: Express the real and map lengths in compatible units first.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate an actual area from a scale drawing.
questions.question: A scale drawing uses scale \(1:50\). A rectangular room measures \(4\text{ cm}\) by \(3\text{ cm}\) on the drawing. What is the actual area of the room?
questions.explanation: The real side lengths are \(4\times 50=200\text{ cm}\) and \(3\times 50=150\text{ cm}\). Convert them: \(200\text{ cm}=2\text{ m}\) and \(150\text{ cm}=1.5\text{ m}\). The area is \(2\times 1.5=3\text{ m}^2\). The alternative \(6\text{ m}^2\) assigns the \(3\text{ cm}\) side a real length of \(3\text{ m}\) instead of \(1.5\text{ m}\).
questions.hint: Express the real and drawing lengths in compatible units first.

questions.concept: Determining a Scale from Drawing and Actual Lengths
questions.learningObjective: Determine the scale of a drawing from an actual length and a drawing length.
questions.question: A building is \(24\text{ m}\) long. In a drawing, it is \(8\text{ cm}\) long. What is the scale of the drawing?
questions.explanation: Convert \(24\text{ m}\) to centimetres: \(24\times 100=2{,}400\text{ cm}\). The scale compares drawing length to actual length: \(8:2{,}400\). Dividing both terms by \(8\) gives \(1:300\). The alternative compares \(8\) centimetres with the numerical metre value \(24\) without converting the units, giving \(8:24=1:3\).
questions.hint: Decide whether you are moving from the drawing to reality or the reverse.

questions.concept: Determining a Map Scale from Two Lengths
questions.learningObjective: Determine a map scale from a map distance and an actual distance.
questions.question: On a map, \(5\text{ cm}\) represents an actual distance of \(2.5\text{ km}\). What is the scale of the map?
questions.explanation: Convert \(2.5\text{ km}\) to centimetres: \(2.5\times 100{,}000=250{,}000\text{ cm}\). The scale compares map length to actual length: \(5:250{,}000\). Dividing both terms by \(5\) gives \(1:50{,}000\). The alternative converts \(2.5\) kilometres only to \(2{,}500\) metres, then compares that value directly with \(5\) centimetres, giving \(5:2{,}500=1:500\).
questions.hint: Express the real and map lengths in compatible units first.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate a drawing length from an actual length using a given scale.
questions.question: A scale drawing uses scale \(1:25\). An actual length is \(3\text{ m}\). What is the length on the drawing in centimetres?
questions.explanation: Convert \(3\text{ m}\) to centimetres: \(3\times 100=300\text{ cm}\). Then divide by the scale factor: \(300\div 25=12\). Thus the drawing length is \(12\text{ cm}\). The alternative \(75\text{ cm}\) multiplies the metre value by \(25\) without first converting it to centimetres.
questions.hint: Express the real and drawing lengths in compatible units first.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate an actual distance from a map distance using a given scale.
questions.question: A map has scale \(1:25{,}000\). A distance on the map is \(8\text{ cm}\). What is the actual distance in kilometres?
questions.explanation: The actual distance in centimetres is \(8\times 25{,}000=200{,}000\text{ cm}\). Since \(100{,}000\text{ cm}=1\text{ km}\), \(200{,}000\text{ cm}=2\text{ km}\). The alternative \(20\text{ km}\) uses \(10{,}000\) centimetres per kilometre instead of \(100{,}000\).
questions.hint: Decide whether you are moving from the drawing to reality or the reverse.

questions.learningObjective: Determine which scale produces a larger drawing for the same real object.
questions.question: For the same real object, which scale produces the larger drawing?
questions.explanation: A scale of \(1:10\) means \(1\text{ cm}\) on the drawing represents \(10\text{ cm}\) in reality, while \(1:100\) means \(1\text{ cm}\) represents \(100\text{ cm}\). The scale \(1:10\) gives a larger drawing for the same real object. The alternative scale makes every drawing length ten times smaller than the first scale.
questions.hint: Compare how long the same real length becomes under each scale.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate an actual area from a map scale.
questions.question: A map has scale \(1:50{,}000\). A rectangular park measures \(6\text{ cm}\) by \(5\text{ cm}\) on the map. What is the actual area of the park in square kilometres?
questions.explanation: The real side lengths are \(6\times 50{,}000=300{,}000\text{ cm}\) and \(5\times 50{,}000=250{,}000\text{ cm}\). Convert them: \(300{,}000\text{ cm}=3\text{ km}\) and \(250{,}000\text{ cm}=2.5\text{ km}\). The area is \(3\times 2.5=7.5\text{ km}^2\). The alternative \(15\text{ km}^2\) assigns the \(5\text{ cm}\) side a real length of \(5\text{ km}\) instead of \(2.5\text{ km}\).
questions.hint: Express the real and drawing lengths in compatible units first.
